title: Deep Brain Stimulation of the Anterior Nucleus of the Thalamus in Drug-Resistant Epilepsy in the MORE Multicenter Patient Registry
article_subtype: Open-label, international observational registry using prospective and retrospective data
condition_or_topic: Anterior nucleus of the thalamus deep brain stimulation (ANT DBS) for drug-resistant focal epilepsy.
clinical_background: Of the 50 million people worldwide with epilepsy, one-third continue to have seizures despite appropriate antiseizure medications. Some patients with drug-resistant epilepsy cannot undergo resective surgery because seizure onset is poorly localized, multifocal, or within eloquent cortex; depending on the underlying pathology, 26%–64% continue to have seizures after epilepsy surgery. The SANTE trial and its extended follow-up demonstrated the efficacy of ANT DBS, but questions remain about which patients are most likely to benefit. Additional single-center studies have limited sample sizes, motivating assessment in routine clinical practice.
objectives: Describe the clinical characteristics of patients receiving ANT DBS in the MORE registry.
Assess the relative change in monthly seizure frequency at 2 years after implantation as the primary effectiveness objective, and examine changes in seizure frequency over follow-up.
Assess health-related quality of life, including Quality of Life in Epilepsy 31-item questionnaire (QOLIE31) scores, and depression using Beck Depression Inventory II (BDI-II) scores.
Characterize adverse events and ANT DBS stimulation parameters through 24 months of follow-up.
Identify factors that may predict treatment response and explore trends associated with changes in seizure frequency.
clinical_question: In adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy receiving ANT DBS, how does monthly seizure frequency at 2 years after implantation compare with the preimplantation baseline?
interpretation: The MORE registry supports the effectiveness and safety of ANT DBS in routine care for patients with DRE and provides Class IV evidence for reduced seizure frequency in drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Median monthly seizure frequency fell by 33.1% after 2 years. Among patients followed for 5 years, the 55.1% reduction suggests that seizure frequency may continue to decline beyond 2 years. Outcomes appeared to vary with center experience and possibly with cognitive status and the region where seizures originate, but differences in median seizure reduction between center-volume groups and between cognitive-status groups were not statistically significant. The authors identified no new safety concerns relative to SANTE. Although QOLIE-31 improved on average, the change did not reach its minimally important clinical difference threshold; BDI scores did not change significantly during active stimulation.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The findings support the effectiveness and safety previously reported by SANTE and single-center studies, although MORE showed a smaller median seizure-frequency reduction at 2 years than the 56.0% reported in the SANTE open-label extension. In SANTE, 54% achieved a reduction of at least 50%, while 10% had an increased seizure count. The apparent continued improvement through 5 years in MORE is consistent with longer-term findings from SANTE and reports concerning VNS and responsive neurostimulation. The authors also consider MORE outcomes comparable with published real-world VNS data describing median seizure reduction of less than 30% by 1 year and more than 50% by 5 years. MORE included smaller proportions of patients with temporal lobe epilepsy than SANTE (39% versus 60%) and larger proportions with diffuse or multifocal epilepsy (24% versus 9%); SANTE had reported greater benefit by 2 years for seizures of temporal origin than for seizures originating elsewhere or from multiple regions. Depression complaints in MORE occurred in 13% over 2 years, compared with 15% during the 3-month double-blind period in the active SANTE group; the corresponding memory-complaint figures were 15% and 13%. Unlike MORE, where no patient discontinued therapy during the first year after implantation, SANTE reported 5 discontinuations during its initial 13-month open-label phase.
clinical_implications: Baseline cognitive impairment and the likely region of seizure origin may help identify patients most likely to benefit from ANT DBS, but the authors regard these as possible selection features rather than established predictors.
Patients without cognitive impairment may be better candidates for ANT DBS, although the observed difference in median seizure reduction was not statistically significant and requires further study.
The greater occurrence of multifocal epilepsy in the no-benefit group suggests that such patients may be less likely to respond.

Center experience may influence seizure outcomes; centers with more than 10 implantations had a 42.8% median monthly seizure reduction at 2 years, compared with 25.8% in centers with 10 or less implantations. The authors describe better outcomes at more experienced centers, while the reported comparison of median reductions was p = NS.
The modest QOLIE-31 change may indicate that quality-of-life measures are insufficiently sensitive to clinically relevant seizure reductions that do not achieve seizure freedom.
practice_implications: ANT DBS or other surgical therapies should probably be considered before adding a third or fourth ASM in patients with DRE, to avoid cognitive, psychiatric, and other ASM-related tolerability effects.
The authors recommend considering ANT DBS before further increasing ASM burden in patients with DRE.

Centers implanting ANT DBS should maintain a comprehensive, long-term commitment to patient selection, implantation, and treatment optimization; the authors also suggest optimizing implantation protocols to improve effectiveness.
limitations: Follow-up visit windows were not protocolized.
Optional HRQOL and BDI questionnaires were completed by only a subset of patients.
Retrospective inclusion of some patients may have introduced selection bias.
Limited sample sizes within the responder, improver, and no-benefit groups may have contributed to the lack of statistical significance for most apparent baseline differences.
strengths: Comprehensive, systematic data collection across multiple centers and countries enabled clinically relevant assessment of patient characteristics, surgery, effectiveness, and safety.
The registry adds routine-practice evidence alongside the SANTE randomized trial.
open_questions: Which patient characteristics best predict benefit from ANT DBS remains unresolved.
Whether cognitive impairment materially affects response to ANT DBS needs further study.
The effects of implantation route, electrode-contact location, and volume of tissue activated on outcomes remain to be examined in detail.
future_directions: Additional exploratory analyses will evaluate the apparent continued reduction in seizure frequency beyond 2 years and be reported separately.
A separate surgical analysis will examine implantation route, contact location, and volume of tissue activated in MORE.
A newly introduced neurostimulator capable of recording local field potentials may help improve understanding and optimization of therapy for patients with DRE.
study_design: MORE was an open-label, international observational registry combining prospective and retrospective clinical data. It evaluated the effectiveness, safety, and device performance of ANT DBS in routine practice. Enrollment ran from February 21, 2012, through April 30, 2017.

population.description: The registry enrolled 191 patients across 25 centers in 13 countries. The effectiveness analysis included 170 patients who met all eligibility criteria and received DBS for epilepsy. Their mean age at baseline was 35.6 ± 10.7 years. Patients had drug-resistant focal epilepsy; seizure types were classified by sites using the ILAE 1981 classification and matched to ILAE 2017 types.
inclusion_criteria: Focal drug-resistant epilepsy documented in a seizure diary.
Failure to benefit from at least 2 ASMs.
A seizure diary covering a minimum of 2 full consecutive calendar months before DBS surgery.
exclusion_criteria: A seizure diary judged incomplete and/or unreliable by the treating physician.
population.care_setting: 25 clinical centers in 13 countries, following routine clinical practice.

interventions: Bilateral ANT DBS implantation using a stereotactic approach. The protocol specified Medtronic Model 3387 DBS leads connected through subcutaneous extensions to a dual-channel Activa PC Neurostimulator, while each DBS center made the final lead selection. Implantation, stimulation settings, and medication adjustments followed local clinical practice.
For patients with an existing VNS system, its management was left to the treating physician's instructions.
comparators: Each patient's seizure frequency before implantation served as the baseline for assessing subsequent change.
Exploratory analyses compared outcomes by baseline cognitive impairment and by center implantation volume.

primary: Relative change in monthly SF at 2 years after implantation.
secondary: Responder status, defined as ≥50% SR; patients with 50% > SR > 0% were categorized as improvers and those with SR ≤0% as having no benefit.
Adverse events, serious adverse events, and device events.
Stimulation parameters and patient-reported outcomes, including HRQOL and cognitive performance.

statistical_methods: Safety analyses used the all patients set (APS), comprising everyone enrolled; effectiveness analyses used the full analysis set (FAS), comprising eligible APS patients implanted with DBS, following the intent to treat (ITT) principle. Baseline and follow-up data were summarized descriptively. Paired changes were assessed with a paired Student t test or an appropriate nonparametric method, including the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Between-group comparisons used the Student test, analysis of variance, or Kruskal-Wallis test for continuous variables and the Fisher exact test for categorical variables. Although no formal hypothesis testing was specified, p values provided context for paired changes. Tests used a 5% significance level without adjustment for multiple comparisons. Missing data were not imputed for primary or secondary effectiveness outcomes. Adverse events were summarized descriptively using the available patients in each period and were classified with Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 22.0; an external committee assessed potential links to DBS devices, programming, or procedures. Analyses used SAS version 9.4.
follow_up: Patients were followed for at least 24 months after enrollment, with visits grouped at 3 months, 6 months, and every 6 months thereafter. An extension to 5 years was introduced in February 2016 but ended when all participants had reached 2 years, before some could reach 5 years.

safety_results.discontinuations: None of the DBS-related serious adverse events led to study discontinuation. No patient discontinued therapy during the first year after implantation. Two subjects underwent explantation because of infection, and one underwent explantation because of suicidal ideation; the report does not give an overall adverse-event discontinuation rate.
safety_results.related_deaths: No deaths were related to DBS. One patient died from definite SUDEP during the second year of follow-up.
notable_adverse_events: Across baseline to 2-year follow-up, 160 serious adverse events were reported in 83 subjects (43.5%); the most frequent serious adverse event was seizure in 18 subjects (10.1%).

During the 2 years after implantation, 59 DBS-related serious adverse events occurred in 42 subjects (23%). The most frequent DBS-related serious adverse event was seizure in 7 subjects (3.9%). DBS-related serious adverse events were linked to the procedure (n = 24), stimulation/programming (n = 21), or implanted system components in 11 subjects (6.1%).

Lead modifications occurred in 11 subjects (6.1%), most often explantation with replacement. Infection prompted 2 explantations in 2 (1%) subjects, and suicidal ideation prompted 1 explantation in 1 subject. No intracranial hemorrhages were reported.

Of the memory impairment complaints, 39% were assessed by sites as worsening of preexisting conditions; the corresponding proportion for depressive mood complaints was 44%. The 24 patients receiving both DBS and VNS were described as having a safety profile similar to that of the remaining population; numerical data were not provided.

subgroup_analyses: Patients receiving both DBS and VNS had a median seizure reduction of 33.1%; this subgroup comprised 24 patients.

At 2 years, patients from 21 centers with 10 or less ANT DBS implantations had a median monthly seizure-frequency reduction of 25.8%, versus 42.8% among patients from 4 centers with more than 10 implantations. The comparison of these median changes was not statistically significant (p = NS).

At 2 years, the responder rate was 22.2% in low-volume centers and 43.2% in high-volume centers (p < 0.05). Most baseline characteristics did not differ significantly between center groups; FIAS was proportionally more frequent at high-volume sites and FBTCS at low-volume sites.
At 2 years, median seizure reduction was 26.0% for patients with baseline cognitive impairment and 36.1% for those without it. The difference was not statistically significant (p = NS).

Responder rates for patients with frontal, temporal, or other seizure-onset zones were around 30%. In the temporal-onset analysis across seizure types, the reported median seizure-frequency change ranged from −27.9% at 1-year to 32.6% at 2-year follow-up. The positive sign of the latter figure conflicts with the accompanying description of a reduction; the report states that changes at each follow-up were significant (all p < 0.05).

Across seizure types, the reported median seizure-frequency changes ranged from −18.4% to −34.7% for frontal-onset seizures and from −17.1% to −24.8% for seizures originating in other lobes; the report states all p < 0.05 at each follow-up.

The responder group contained numerically more patients with temporal lobe epilepsy than the no-benefit group, while multifocal epilepsy was more frequent in the no-benefit group than among responders. Most apparent differences in baseline characteristics across responders, improvers, and no-benefit patients did not reach statistical significance.
secondary_results: The registry recruited 191 patients across 25 centers in 13 countries, with 1 to 28 patients recruited per site. Of these, 170 were implanted and met all eligibility criteria; 157 (92.4%) of the 170 completed the visit scheduled around 2 years after implantation. Median follow-up was 2 years.

In the full analysis set, mean ± SD baseline age was 35.6 ± 10.7 years, 73 (42.9) were female, mean ± SD epilepsy duration was 23.1 ± 12.1 years, and median baseline monthly seizure frequency was 15.8 (0–610).

At baseline, cognitive impairment was reported in 64 (37.6) patients and mood disorders in 36 (21.2). A prior VNS implant was reported in 73 (42.9), and prior resective brain surgery for epilepsy in 34 (20.0). The surgical-history categories were neither procedure, 77 (45.3); VNS only, 59 (34.7); prior resective surgery only, 20 (11.8); and both, 14 (8.2).

Among the 73 patients with a previous VNS implant, 28 (38%) had it explanted before DBS implantation. Of those who still had VNS at DBS implantation, 24 (53%) continued VNS therapy during registry data collection.

For total prior and current ASMs at baseline, the measure was available in 170 (100.0) patients; mean ± SD was 8.7 ± 3.2 and median (minimum–maximum) was 9.0 (3–19). At implantation, the ASM-count measure was available in 170 (100.0): 0 ASMs in 5 (2.9), 1 in 10 (5.9), 2 in 34 (20.0), 3 in 68 (40.0), and ≥4 in 53 (31.2). Mean ± SD was 3.0 ± 1.1 and median (minimum–maximum) was 3.0 (0–7).

For epilepsy type under ILAE 2017, data were available in 170 (100.0): focal epilepsies, 164 (96.5); epilepsies and syndromes undetermined as to focal or generalized, 3 (1.8); and other, 3 (1.8). Reported seizure types were FIASs in 146 (85.9), FBTCSs in 109 (64.1), FASs in 67 (39.4), and other in 5 (2.9).

The most likely seizure-origin region was documented for 170 (100.0): unifocal temporal, 66 (38.8); frontal, 30 (17.6); parietal, 7 (4.1); occipital, 9 (5.3); unknown, 2 (1.2); multifocal bitemporal only, 0 (0.0); diffuse or multifocal, 41 (24.1); and multilobar, 15 (8.8).
Baseline monthly seizure-count categories were 0–5 in 32 (18.8) patients, >5–15 in 52 (30.6), >15–30 in 36 (21.2), >30–90 in 32 (18.8), and >90 in 18 (10.6).
Nearly all patients (94%) received an Activa PC stimulator; the most frequently implanted bilateral lead model was 3389, used in 76%.
In the 5-year follow-up subgroup, median change from baseline in monthly seizure frequency was −6.3 (−114.7, 488.9) at 2-y follow-up and −8.0 (−119.8, 224.8) at 5-y follow-up.

At 2 years, the mean QOLIE-31 score improved by 2 points (p < 0.05), and about one-third of patients improved by ≥5 points (p = 0.02). QOLIE-31 measures were available for 78 patients; the reported improvement did not meet the minimally important clinical difference threshold.
No statistically significant change in depression prevalence or severity was observed across visits (p > 0.05 for all visits). BDI scoring was available for 87 patients.
Over 2 years, amplitude, pulse width, stimulation frequency, and the percentage of patients receiving intermittent cycling stimulation did not change significantly.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that the multinational MORE registry adds real-world support for the safety and effectiveness of ANT DBS in DRE. They identify cognitive impairment and likely seizure-onset region as possible considerations for patient selection, advise considering ANT DBS before further increasing ASM burden, and emphasize sustained center involvement in selection, implantation and treatment optimization.
narrative_summary: MORE was an open-label, international observational registry examining ANT DBS in routine care for patients with DRE. It enrolled 191 patients across 25 centers in 13 countries; 170 met eligibility criteria and received an implant. In the full analysis set, median monthly seizure frequency fell from 15.8 at baseline to 8.8 at 2 years, a median reduction of 33.1% (p < 0.0001), and the responder rate was 32.3%. Among 47 patients with 5 years of follow-up, median monthly seizure frequency declined from 16.0 at baseline to 7.9 at 5 years, with a median reduction of 55.1% (p < 0.0001). Patients with baseline cognitive impairment had a smaller median reduction at 2 years than those without it, but the difference was not statistically significant. Outcomes also varied by implantation-center experience. Frequently reported adverse events included seizure changes, memory complaints and depressive mood; 59 DBS-related serious adverse events occurred in 42 subjects (23%) during the 2 years after implantation. One definite SUDEP occurred during the second year, with no deaths attributed to DBS. The authors regard these findings as supporting effectiveness and safety while noting limitations from seizure diaries, nonprotocolized visits, optional questionnaires and partly retrospective enrollment. They recommend sustained attention to patient selection, implantation and therapy optimization, and considering ANT DBS before further increasing ASM burden. The study provides Class IV evidence for seizure-frequency reduction.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: The double-blind SANTE randomized controlled trial established the efficacy of ANT DBS in DRE. MORE was designed to examine longer-term effectiveness and safety in routine care.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: MORE combined prospectively and retrospectively collected observational data. Patients aged at least 18 years with focal DRE were recruited at 25 centers in 13 countries. Follow-up lasted at least 2 years and assessed SF, RR, health-related quality of life with Quality of Life in Epilepsy Inventory 31, depression, and safety.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: Of 191 recruited patients, 170 received DBS and fulfilled eligibility criteria; their mean (SD) age was 35.6 (10.7) years, and 43% were female. At baseline, 38% reported cognitive impairment. Median monthly SF fell 33.1%, from 15.8 at baseline to 8.8 at 2 years (p < 0.0001); RR was 32.3%. Among 47 patients followed for 5 years, median monthly SF fell 55.1%, from 16 at baseline to 7.9 at 5 years (p < 0.0001), with 53.2% RR. At 2 years, median monthly SF reductions were 42.8% at high-volume centers (>10 implantations) and 25.8% at low-volume centers; corresponding reductions were 26.0% in patients with cognitive impairment and 36.1% in those without it. The most frequently reported adverse events were changes in seizure frequency or severity (16%), patient-reported memory impairment (15%), patient-reported depressive mood (13%), and epilepsy (12%). One definite SUDEP occurred.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors interpret MORE as supporting the effectiveness and safety of ANT DBS during the 2 years after implantation in routine clinical care.

document_sections.heading: Classification of Evidence
document_sections.content: The authors assign Class IV evidence to the finding that ANT DBS reduces seizure frequency in drug-resistant focal epilepsy.

document_sections.heading: Trial Registration Information
document_sections.content: MORE was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT01521754 and was first posted on January 31, 2012.

document_sections.heading: Deep Brain Stimulation of the Anterior Nucleus of the Thalamus in Drug-Resistant Epilepsy in the MORE Multicenter Patient Registry
document_sections.content: Worldwide, 50 million people have epilepsy, and one-third continue having seizures despite appropriate ASMs. Resective surgery is unsuitable for many people with DRE because seizure onset is poorly localized, multifocal, or situated in eloquent cortex. Depending on pathology, 26%–64% continue having seizures after epilepsy surgery. Neuromodulation, including DBS, is an option for these patients. The pivotal SANTE trial and its 10 years of extended follow-up demonstrated ANT DBS efficacy in DRE, but the best candidates remain uncertain. Single-center studies also support its safety and efficacy, although their small samples limit generalizability; consensus guidance combines those studies, SANTE, and expert opinion. The authors therefore established a large multinational registry that could include difficult-to-treat focal epilepsy and comorbidities, as well as physician-selected targeting methods and leads not assessed in earlier studies. Its primary questions concerned patient characteristics, changes in SF and HRQOL, AEs, and stimulation parameters through 24 months.

document_sections.heading: Study Design
document_sections.content: MORE was an international, open-label observational registry using prospective and retrospective data to evaluate longer-term effectiveness, safety, and device performance for ANT DBS in DRE. It was intended to characterize implanted patients, investigate predictors of response and trends in SF, and assess patient-reported HRQOL and cognitive performance. Center selection partly reflected previous expertise in DRE resective surgery or DBS for other indications and access to enough potentially eligible patients.

document_sections.heading: Participants
document_sections.content: Eligible patients were at least 18 years old, had focal DRE documented in a seizure diary, and had failed to benefit from at least 2 ASMs. Sites initially classified seizures using ILAE 1981 terminology; Table 1 presents matching ILAE 2017 seizure types. When seizure and epilepsy classifications disagreed, the primary and last authors reassessed available clinical and EEG information. Patients were excluded if follow-up was impracticable or the treating physician judged their seizure diaries incomplete or unreliable. Treating physicians were advised to manage any existing VNS according to its instructions. Less than one-third enrolled a median of 12.6 months after implantation; their available baseline and follow-up SF information was collected retrospectively. Enrollment did not require consecutive patients.

document_sections.heading: Surgical and Clinical Procedure
document_sections.content: Before DBS surgery, patients needed seizure diaries covering at least 2 complete consecutive calendar months. At baseline, diary information and eligibility criteria were checked again. Implantation followed each physician’s usual practice. The protocol specified CE-marked Medtronic Model 3387 DBS leads connected through subcutaneous extensions to a dual-channel Activa PC Neurostimulator, although each center made the final lead choice. Stereotactic implantation targeted both anterior thalamic nuclei, with postoperative MRI and/or CT used to check lead position. Operating centers decided whether reimplantation was needed. Centers determined stimulation timing and dose and medication changes according to local practice, principally informed by SANTE practice. Enrolled patients were followed for at least 24 months. A 5-year extension began in February 2016 after some patients had left the original study and ended when everyone had reached 2 years, before some could reach 5 years. Visits followed routine care and were grouped at 3 months, 6 months, and every 6 months thereafter. Under ISO 14155:2011, any change in symptom frequency or severity required AE or device-event reporting. Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 22.0 was used to classify events, including worsening seizures or epilepsy. An external committee assessed possible links to DBS devices, programming, or procedures. Medications were coded with World Health Organization Drug version 2b2016SEP.

document_sections.heading: Standard Protocol Approvals, Registrations, and Patient Consents
document_sections.content: The registry followed the Declaration of Helsinki and applicable national rules, including data-protection requirements. Each center obtained ethics approval except those in Poland, where local rules did not require it. All participants provided approved informed or data-release consent. ClinicalTrials.gov registration NCT01521754 occurred on January 31, 2012.

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analysis Methods
document_sections.content: APS included everyone enrolled and served as the safety population. FAS comprised APS patients who met every eligibility criterion and received DBS for epilepsy, following the ITT principle. FAS supported the primary effectiveness analysis of relative monthly SF change at 2 years after implantation and secondary analyses including QOLIE-31 and BDI-II scores. Missing values were not imputed for these objectives. At 2 years, patients were classified as responders (≥50% SR), improvers (50% > SR > 0%), or having no benefit (SR ≤0%). Baseline and follow-up data were summarized descriptively. The study specified no formal hypothesis tests; reported p values instead provided context for paired changes. Depending on suitability, paired changes were examined with a paired Student t test or nonparametric method such as the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Between-group continuous-variable comparisons used the Student test, analysis of variance, or Kruskal-Wallis test; categorical comparisons used Fisher exact test. Tests used a 5% significance level without adjustment for multiple comparisons. Safety analyses were descriptive, with period-specific AEs assessed among patients available during each period. Analyses used SAS version 9.4.

document_sections.heading: Data Availability
document_sections.content: Individual patient data cannot be routinely shared outside the MORE study group, even in coded form, because consent for that sharing was not obtained and local law prevents release. The MORE publication committee will evaluate requests for statistical-analysis syntax and output.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: Enrollment ran from February 21, 2012, through April 30, 2017; the final data were collected on June 19, 2019. Across 25 centers in 13 countries, 191 patients entered APS, with sites recruiting 1 to 28 patients each. Of 170 FAS patients, 157 (92.4%) attended follow-up visit 5, scheduled around 2 years after implantation; median follow-up was 2 years. Figure 1 describes disposition and reasons why 13 patients withdrew before that visit. Its notes identify 4 patients enrolled before site accreditation, 7 who completed and reported 2-year visits before the 5-year follow-up extension, 2 whose devices were removed without replacement because of infection, and a death judged unrelated to DBS by an external advisory committee.

document_sections.heading: Baseline Characteristics (FAS)
document_sections.content: Mean (SD) age was 35.6 (10.7) years, and 43% were female. Under the 1989 ILAE syndrome classification, 96% had localization-related, or focal, epilepsy. Mean (SD) epilepsy duration was 23.1 (12.1) years; baseline median monthly SF was 15.8. Monthly seizures numbered 5 or fewer in 32 patients and more than 90 in 18. Most had FIASs (86%) or FBTCSs (64%). The median number of previously tried or current ASMs at baseline was 9. Before ANT DBS, 34 (20%) had undergone at least 1 resective epilepsy operation, and 73 (43%) had received a VNS implant. Of those with prior VNS, 28 (38%) had it removed before DBS. Among patients retaining VNS when DBS was implanted, 24 (53%) continued VNS during MORE data collection. At entry, 38% reported cognitive impairment and 21% had mood disorders. Nearly all patients (94%) received an Activa PC stimulator; model 3389 was the most common bilateral lead, implanted in 76%. Table 1 details demographic, psychosocial, treatment-history, ASM, epilepsy-type, seizure-type, onset-region, and baseline seizure-count characteristics.

document_sections.heading: Outcomes
document_sections.content: Median monthly SF declined progressively from 15.8 at baseline to 8.8 at 2 years, a median reduction of 33.1% (p < 0.0001). Responders accounted for 32.3%, including 5 patients without seizures at 2 years. The 24 patients receiving both DBS and VNS had a similar median reduction of 33.1%. Among 47 patients with an additional 3 years of observation, median SR was 43.3% at 2 years and 55.1% at 5 years; RR rose from 40.4% to 53.2%. Table 2 details seizure-frequency measurements, changes from baseline, percentage changes, and p values for this subgroup. Figure 2 describes a 101%–6,519% range of increased median monthly SF among patients whose increase exceeded 100%. At 2 years, patients at 21 low-volume centers with 10 or fewer ANT DBS implantations had a 25.8% median monthly SF reduction, versus 42.8% at 4 high-volume centers with more than 10 implantations (p = NS). Patients with baseline cognitive impairment had 26.0% median SR, versus 36.1% in those without it (p = NS). Most apparent baseline differences between responders, improvers, and patients with no benefit were not statistically significant, potentially because each group was small. RR was around 30% for frontal, temporal, and other onset zones. Across seizure types, the reported median SF change for temporal-origin seizures ranged from −27.9% at 1-year follow-up to 32.6% at 2-year follow-up; reductions for frontal-origin seizures ranged from −18.4% to −34.7%, and for seizures originating in other lobes from −17.1% to −24.8% (all p < 0.05 at each follow-up). At 2 years, RR was 43.2% at high-volume centers and 22.2% at low-volume centers (p < 0.05). Of 155 patients with 2-year information, 50 were responders: 32 (64%) from high-volume centers and 18 (36%) from low-volume centers. Most baseline variables did not differ significantly by center-volume group, except that high-volume centers had more FIAS and low-volume centers more FBTCS. Mean QOLIE-31 improved by 2 points overall (p < 0.05); about one-third improved ≥5 points at 2 years (p = 0.02). QOLIE-31 data were available for only 78 patients. Neither depression prevalence nor severity changed significantly (p > 0.05 for all visits); BDI scores were available for only 87. During 2 years, amplitude, pulse width, stimulation frequency, and the proportion using intermittent cycling did not change significantly. The most reported AEs were changes in seizure frequency or severity (16%), patient-reported memory impairment (15%), patient-reported depressive mood (13%), and epilepsy (12%). Site assessments attributed 39% of memory complaints and 44% of depressive-mood complaints to deterioration of preexisting conditions. Other AEs were headache (7%), head injury (5%), irritability (5%), anxiety (5%), and cognitive impairment (5%). Table 3 presents period-specific AEs affecting ≥3% of APS patients; its notes also describe DBS-related infections affecting <3% and types of device dislocation. The 24 patients receiving both DBS and VNS had a safety profile similar to the remainder, although supporting data are not shown. From baseline through 2 years, 83 patients (43.5%) experienced 160 SAEs; seizure was the most frequent, occurring in 18 (10.1%). The study classified SAEs involving the procedure, lead, neurostimulator, extension, another DBS component, or programming or stimulation as DBS-related. In the 2 years after implantation, 42 patients (23%) experienced 59 DBS-related SAEs; none caused study discontinuation. Seizure was the most frequent DBS-related SAE, affecting 7 (3.9%). DBS-related SAEs were linked to the procedure (n = 24), stimulation or programming (n = 21), or implanted components (11 [6.1%]). Lead modifications occurred in 11 patients (6.1%), most often removal with replacement. Infection prompted 2 removals in 2 (1%) patients, and suicidal ideation prompted 1 removal in 1 patient. There were no intracranial hemorrhages or DBS-related deaths. During the second follow-up year, 1 patient died from definite SUDEP.

document_sections.heading: Classification of Evidence
document_sections.content: The authors classify the evidence that ANT DBS reduces seizure frequency in drug-resistant focal epilepsy as Class IV.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors consider MORE a systematic multinational source of routine-care evidence on ANT DBS in DRE. Its findings support efficacy and safety previously reported by SANTE and single-center studies: median monthly SF fell 33.1% after 2 years, although outcomes varied with center experience. No new procedure- or treatment-related safety concern emerged relative to SANTE. Among those reaching 5 years, SR was 55.1%; the authors say this suggests further SF reduction beyond 2 years, consistent with SANTE and reports concerning VNS and responsive neurostimulation. They indicate that additional exploratory work will assess that trend. At 2 years in MORE, median monthly SF was 8.8 rather than the baseline 15.8, a 33.1% median reduction across seizure types. Approximately 32% responded, 29% had no SF reduction, and the remainder improved without reaching 50% SR. The SANTE open-label extension reported a greater median SF reduction of 56.0%; 54% achieved at least 50% reduction, while 10% had increased seizure counts. By comparison, cited real-world VNS data reported median SR below 30% by 1 year and above 50% by 5 years. The authors identify 5 potentially clinically relevant influences on SR. First, cognitive impairment was associated with numerically smaller median monthly SR at 2 years—26.0% versus 36.1% without impairment—but this difference was not statistically significant. SANTE excluded patients with IQ below 70. A cited single-center ANT DBS study found lower response likelihood with cognitive impairment, particularly executive-function impairment; cited pediatric VNS research reported similar findings. MORE therefore suggests that patients without cognitive impairment may be better candidates, but further study is needed. Second, seizure-onset region may matter: temporal lobe epilepsy was numerically more common among MORE responders than among patients with no benefit. Temporal lobe epilepsy accounted for 39% in MORE versus 60% in SANTE, while frontal, parietal, and occipital proportions were similar. Multifocal epilepsy appeared more often among MORE patients without benefit than among responders, suggesting potentially lower response likelihood. Diffuse or multifocal epilepsy accounted for 24% in MORE versus 9% in SANTE. In SANTE, temporal-origin seizures had relatively greater stimulation benefit by 2 years than seizures from other lobes or multiple regions. Third, greater variability of baseline SF in MORE, despite similar baseline medians to SANTE, may have affected outcomes; MORE also had more varied seizure types, potentially reflecting difficulties with classification in routine care. Fourth, a median of 9 failed ASMs in MORE suggested pronounced refractoriness. SANTE required at least 3 failed ASMs but did not report the total tried. MORE patients used a median of 3 concurrent ASMs versus 2 in SANTE; the authors suggest that greater ASM burden could influence seizure outcomes. Prior or current resective surgery and VNS, epilepsy duration, and implantation age were otherwise similar between studies. To avoid cognitive, psychiatric, and other ASM-related tolerability effects, the authors say ANT DBS or other surgical therapies should probably be considered before adding the third or fourth ASM in DRE. Fifth, centers with more than 10 implants achieved better seizure outcomes than those with 10 or fewer: median monthly SR was 42.8% versus 25.8%. MORE permitted transventricular and extraventricular routes and lead models 3387 and 3389; SANTE used only a transventricular route and model 3387 and centrally evaluated targeting. An earlier MORE surgical analysis found different ANT-area target locations between the 2 approaches. The authors plan separate analyses of route, contact location, and activated tissue volume. Stimulation protocols were similar for most patients across MORE and SANTE, although MORE did not specify stimulation-parameter requirements. The authors infer that centers should remain committed to optimizing implantation protocols. They regard routine-care studies as especially reliable for safety information because tolerability may be recorded more precisely than effectiveness, while randomized trials have restrictions on patient inclusion. Depression and memory-complaint rates in MORE were broadly consistent with SANTE’s early follow-up: depression was reported by 13% across 2 years in MORE versus 15% in SANTE’s active group during its 3-month double-blind phase; memory impairment was reported by 15% across 2 years in MORE versus 13% during SANTE’s active-stimulation double-blind phase. Available MORE BDI scores did not differ significantly between baseline and active stimulation. Serious complications causing treatment discontinuation were uncommon in MORE. Nobody discontinued therapy during its first postimplantation year, whereas 5 SANTE patients discontinued during the initial 13-month open-label phase. In MORE’s second year, 1 patient died from confirmed SUDEP; 3 could not be followed (1 lost to follow-up and 2 withdrawn by treating-physician decision without a specified reason), and 2 more withdrew potentially because of infections. Over the corresponding period, 3 SANTE patients discontinued. MORE’s HRQOL results did not reach the minimally important clinical difference threshold for QOLIE-31. The authors note cited studies suggesting seizure freedom, rather than a partial SF reduction, substantially affects HRQOL measures; questionnaires may consequently miss clinically meaningful reductions short of seizure freedom. A cited Delphi consensus found that physicians preferred unstructured interviews over formal questionnaires for assessing ANT DBS effects on HRQOL. Declared strengths are comprehensive, systematic data collection across multiple countries and centers, a clinically practical assessment of patient characteristics, surgery, effectiveness, and safety, and routine-care evidence complementary to SANTE. Declared limitations are potentially unreliable seizure diaries, visit timing without protocol-defined windows, and optional HRQOL and BDI questionnaires completed by only subsets to preserve routine practice. Partly retrospective inclusion may also have introduced selection bias. DBS devices continue to change: SANTE used Kinetra, whereas MORE used Activa PC; the authors suggest that a newer neurostimulator able to record local field potentials might improve understanding and treatment optimization. In conclusion, the authors state that MORE reinforces safety evidence for ANT DBS and confirms treatment effectiveness. They regard cognitive impairment and probable seizure-onset region as possible patient-selection features. They recommend considering ANT DBS in DRE before increasing ASM burden to avoid additional adverse effects and say implantation centers should maintain long-term, comprehensive involvement in patient selection, implantation, and treatment optimization.
